newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss citizens start fund for Holocaust victims.
newsitem.headline: Swiss citizens start fund for Holocaust victims.

text.p: Swiss acadamics, writers and politicians on Friday unveiled a private aid fund for Holocuast victims, independent of efforts by the Swiss government and banks to defuse criticism of the country's role in World War Two.
A committee of personalities, many from universities and the media, urged Swiss citizens to donate and said it hoped to collect one million Swiss francs ($686,000) in a first stage.

"Many people in our country share our view that Switzerland did not get through the years of (Hitler's) Third Reich and the Second World War with as much innocence as we had long believed," it said in a statement.

Switzerland is under pressure from world Jewish groups to make amends for what critics say was cynical profiteering from the war, including buying stolen Nazi gold and sitting on bank accounts left by Jews killed in the Holocaust.
Swiss banks last week pledged 100 million Swiss francs for Holocaust victims as a sign of good faith while they hunt for lost Jewish accounts.

The organisers of the private aid drive, dubbed the "Fund for Humanity and Justice," said Swiss people wanted to take a direct role in addressing historic dark spots rather than leaving this to the government and companies.
"A big part of the Swiss population has the honest intention of uncovering past injustices and redressing them to the extent possible," the statement said.

It said the fund was aimed at providing rapid and uncomplicated aid to impoverished Holocaust survivors, especially in eastern Europe. Those helped could include Jews as well as other people persecuted by the Nazis.

A spokesman said the fund had already chosen two existing projects it intended to support -- help for Jews in the Belarus capital of Minsk and research in the file of the Jewish Historical Institute in Warsaw.
The committee's 21 members include architect Mario Botta, who built the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and Josef Candalfi, the retired Roman Catholic auxilliary bishop of Basle.
